A close reading for the week

“If music be the food of love”

Twelfth Night · Act 1, Scene 1

The play opens with a duke, an orchestra and a theory of desire. Within seven lines Orsino has tested the theory on himself and proved it, in the least flattering way possible.

DUKEIf music be the food of love, play on,
Give me excess of it; that, surfeiting,
The appetite may sicken and so die.1
That strain again, it had a dying fall;2

  1. 1

    A cure by overdose

    The famous first line is a conditional, and the request is stranger than its fame suggests. Orsino asks music to kill his love by feeding it: gorge the appetite until it sickens. He wants to be free of a feeling he is also luxuriating in, and the speech’s comedy and pathos lie in that contradiction, announced before the play is three lines old.

  2. 2

    The dying fall

    A “fall” is a cadence, the phrase of melody that sinks to its close, and “dying” makes the technical term languish. Orsino asks for one strain to be repeated: he is curating his own melancholy, replaying the saddest bar. Fashionable Elizabethan gentlemen cultivated love-melancholy as a mark of refinement; Shakespeare gives the fashion an orchestra.
